extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory, constitutional scholars, and informed general readers interested in comparative government
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic comparison of Parliamentary and Presidential constitutions, focusing on how each system generates discussion, accountability, fiscal outcomes, and the roles of dignified vs efficient parts of government. Draws on 19th-century British observations about American experience (Civil War era).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary government: discussion and public participation
rubrics_metrics.description: The distinguishing quality of Parliamentary Government is, that in each stage of a public transaction there is a discussion; that the public assist at this discussion; that it can, through Parliament, turn out an administration which is not doing as it likes, and can put in an administration which will do as it likes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parliamentary systems produce continuous public scrutiny and the practical ability to replace administrations; these mechanisms popularise views (through incessant small motions and debate) and force lessons (e.g., fiscal reform) upon the nation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential government: weak public discussion and executive autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: The characteristic of a Presidential Government is, in a multitude of cases, that there is no such discussion; that when there is a discussion the fate of Government does not turn upon it, and, therefore, the people do not attend to it; that, upon the whole, the administration itself is pretty much doing as it likes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because debate does not regularly determine executive survival, Presidential systems may allow administrations to act with less continuous public correction; extraordinary blunders may still provoke public reaction and removal at election times, but day-to-day discussion is weaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for deliberative selection of executives
rubrics_metrics.description: The electoral college was intended to be a deliberative body; letting the election of the President depend on a great popular vote for that sole purpose makes representatives pledged to a single question and diminishes deliberation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting executives through bodies that consider multiple questions (e.g., elected Houses deciding collectively) is recommended to preserve deliberation and avoid single-issue pledging; the Senate's election by state legislatures produced more considered influence in Bagehot's view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public discussion as a check on financial and policy errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Parliamentary Government, public and parliamentary discussion will quickly search into and effectually frustrate financial errors; the whole force of the greatest inquiring and discussing machine will be directed to a subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: errors such as issuing inconvertible paper or ill-considered taxation would have been exposed sooner under Parliament; continuous debate educates the public and forces corrective policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of inconvertible government paper as sole circulating medium
rubrics_metrics.description: Making inconvertible paper notes issued by the Treasury the sole circulating medium (the Legal Tender Act) is a capital error: it tends to be issued in great quantities, to be depreciated as against coin, to disturb values, to derange markets, and to defraud the lender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences include domestic depreciation, distorted prices, loss of foreign credit (preventing borrowing abroad), and impaired information flows from commercial houses; prudence requires maintaining credible currency and foreign credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity to implement direct and internal taxation
rubrics_metrics.description: A government must have the administrative machinery and public habituation to direct/internal taxation; lack of experience causes delay, poor estimates, and weak revenue collection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: American experience: initial avoidance of internal taxation produced late and inadequate revenue; estimates of potential internal receipts vastly exceeded actual collections (example: estimated $85,000,000 vs actual $37,000,000), showing the need for administrative competence and experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid taxing everything indiscriminately ('wherever you see a head, hit it')
rubrics_metrics.description: The expedient of taxing every article, product, trade, profession, or source of income to obtain revenue quickly is a poor principle; it produces excessive and injudicious taxation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under Parliamentary systems such indiscriminate taxation would be argued against and checked; in practice the American wartime system taxed widely and heavily, with exemptions and graduated rates that produced onerous burdens and undesirable economic distortions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity of taxation to national economic character
rubrics_metrics.description: A country's capacity to bear taxation depends on its economic character (e.g., America is unusually insensitive to taxes because it is very rich and productive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy that might be impracticable in one country (maintaining a large surplus via heavy taxation) may be tolerable in another; constitutional designers should account for economic context when assessing fiscal rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for parliamentary scrutiny of surpluses and debt-reduction policy
rubrics_metrics.description: No Parliament would permit an executive to keep a surplus of magnitude without discussion; Parliament compels examination of whether maintaining a surplus (and sustaining high taxation to reduce debt) is wise or injurious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parliamentary debate prevents long-term fiscal injustice (e.g., retaining taxes contrary to free-trade maxims, creating artificial protected industries) by exposing harmful consequences and popularising corrective doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequence assessment of fiscal policy on industry and capital
rubrics_metrics.description: High taxation and protective duties may foster industries that should not exist, displace natural industry, and later cause depreciation and loss of fixed capital when fostering taxes are withdrawn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional and fiscal systems should consider long-term structural effects of taxes (distorted incentives, artificial trade, eventual deprecation of capital) rather than merely short-term revenue needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between 'dignified' and 'efficient' parts of a constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutions have two parts: those which excite and preserve the reverence of the population ('dignified' parts) and the efficient parts which in fact work and rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dignified parts secure authority and loyalty (they 'raise the army' by attracting motive power) though they may not carry out day-to-day business; efficient parts employ the power. Both are necessary: a polity without dignified elements risks lacking the force that underpins governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutions must win authority then use it
rubrics_metrics.description: Every constitution must first gain authority (loyalty and confidence) and then use that authority; success depends on both winning homage and employing it in government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers should not discard ceremonially authoritative institutions as 'useless' — their role in mobilising obedience and legitimacy is a prerequisite for the efficient machinery to function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of literal application of 'division of powers' and 'checks and balances' doctrines
rubrics_metrics.description: The common description that legislative, executive, and judicial powers are quite divided and non-interfering, or that Britain is governed by a balanced union of monarchical, aristocratic, and democratic elements, is often erroneous and inapplicable in different contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical and practical realities produce overlaps and evolving functions; constitutional theory must account for living practice rather than rely on inapt inherited maxims. Imitability is limited where cultural sentiments (e.g., reverence for monarchy) do not exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutions must reflect unequal development within the population
rubrics_metrics.description: Large communities contain strata at very different stages of development; constitutions must remember and address the palpable differences among social classes and regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political theory that ignores these inequalities will be misleading; institutions (particularly dignified parts) help reconcile varied levels of civic culture and make government acceptable across strata.
